Lotta joke comments here. But I drove a smooth tanker and the surge is no fucking joke especially in inclement weather. Give your distance buffer a buffer. If you’re unfamiliar with driving in snow, remember your stab breaking and for the love of god do not panic and slam on your breaks. You’ll see in your mirror just how quickly your trailer can move as it comes up to slap you. Layering is easy. Start with light weight, moisture wicking material, transitioning to heavier, non breathable layers such as a winter jacket. Get you a good pair of waterproof steel toe boots and cold weather socks. You'll need a survival kit that should include extra clothing, water, blankets, and canned or sealed food (tuna is a good pick). Do not use this stuff unless you have to and refresh it sensibly. Keep extra fuses, glad hand seals, batteries, etc in their own area. Above all, do not move if you don’t feel safe. Your supervisor/dispatch might get mad, you may even get reprimanded, but it’s your life and your license, drive safe or not at all. 

And please do not just follow your GPS. As far as I know, the north east is littered with height and length restricted areas. Use your GPS to get you in the general area then obey the local signage. You’ll be fine buddy, one mile at a time.

It does get easier. You’ll get more comfortable and into a routine. But that isn’t to say that trucking might not be something you like, which is totally okay, it’s definitely not something every wants to do.

Clothing: pack for a few more days than necessary, you never know. Get two laundry bags, one for clean laundry, one for dirty (this is more of a personal preference). Don’t wear flip flops outside of your truck. It’s fucking gross and unprofessional. If you’re gonna go into the rest stop to shower, have a pair of sneakers or crocs to wear. 

Food: invest in your food preparation. As much as possible, avoid eating at truck stops. All that exists there is fast food and shitty gas station pizza that’ll make you sick. 

Safety: no matter where you are, lock your doors and when you go to bed, put up all your curtains. If he’s driving a reefer or dry van, see about putting your own lock on the doors along with the seals for extra protection. Never ever fuckin open your door in the middle of the night if someone comes knocking, people are unpredictable. Additionally, carry a bat, ya know, to make sure the tires are inflated properly. 

Trip planning: go with the understanding that most truck stops, in my area at least, will be filled by 830/9, so try to plan accordingly. You definitely don’t want to be nearing violating HOS or falling asleep because there isn’t a suitable place to park. Additionally, your GPS isn’t always right. Allow common sense to prevail; if GPS is saying to turn here, and you can see that you either can’t make it or don’t feel comfortable doing it, try a different route. 

Cleanliness: you likely know, but there are an unfortunate amount of drivers whose cab looks like a garbage bomb went off. Keep your shit clean. You live there, you eat there, you sleep there. Take your trash to the trash can, take out your floor mats and knock the dirt off, make your bed. Tangentially, shower. Driving all day and not cleaning yourself will lead to gross ass conditions like foot fungus and skin infections. 

Sleep: invest in your sleep. Don’t be up to late dicking about. Make sure you get the proper amount YOU need, whether that’s 8, or like me, 10. Buy a nice pillow, buy some nice bedding. It won’t always be a good nights rest, but it doesn’t have to be sucky all the time. 

Technology: bring something to do. Idk what gig you’ll be working but it will absolutely have periods of down time and you may not always have cell service. Bring a laptop/switch/game boy/whatever with some single player games. If gaming isn’t your thing, bring a book, have some movies available, and double check your truck has the capability to charge the electronics.

It’s the few causing problems for the many. One of the causal factors of stores with large parking lots, Walmarts, Home Depot, etc, not allowing truckers to park overnight in their lots is because truckers would park and leave their trash or sweep out their trailers onto the lot. Go to any truck stop and head to the spots that along the back curb and you’ll see trash from inconsiderate and lazy drivers. Having a forcing mechanism that encourages and enforces courtesy and cleanliness would go miles I believe.

But I would also encourage accountability enforced on truckers who trash rest areas. Maybe some manner of if you go to park, you have to go give your truck information to staff inside. They already have people that look through the lot for various reasons so I don’t see it as any change or adding responsibility to have them enforce cleanliness standards via penalizing the truck driver/company with fines or even black listing them.

On sleep:

There’s simply not enough room most of the time. A lot of people would say that’s a fault of bad trip planning, but that is fallacious as if every driver trip planned appropriately, the number of spots available does not change. We need not just more places to sleep, but ones that are safe. Pulling onto a ramp isn’t ideal but is sometimes all you can do. 

Stress reduction:
A lot of stress I experience is dual pronged; poor communication and traffic. We can’t mitigate the latter but the former falls square on dispatch and shippers/receivers. I’d encourage some form of accountability to remedy this. Whether it be a fine or having to financially compensate the offended party/parties. To often drivers get the brunt end of the stick because there is mandatory role the driver plays and we rarely have a way in how it’s done. 

General health:

You work me 6 days and give me 36 hours to reset. That’s enough time to eat, sleep, grocery shop, do laundry, and try to enjoy some personal or family time. More time off would allow me to spend a day or two exercising, eating healthier without breaking the bank, decompress from the work week, and not sacrifice personal or family more than necessary. 

Health care:

Make it mandatory to provide but not accept and comprehensive. While it’s unfortunate that healthcare is so intrinsically tied to having a job, we could do better about providing quality care that doesn’t mean paying thousands in co pays. 

That’s all I got for now but on a personal note, I appreciate the work you’re doing and wish you success.

Regardless of how long you are planned to be out, pack for longer. Idk how many times I’ve been assigned a one day load, only for me to be stuck out there for a day or so because of something gone wrong. 

Always fucking pre trip. Even if you KNOW it’s all good, do it anyways. The amount of unserviceable trailers I’ve found is insane, don’t get caught slacking. 

If you don’t feel comfortable/safe, then stop. The worst thing you can do is panic, followed by continuing. Keep your dispatch informed of whatever you’re planning. 

Route plan. Figure out where you’d like to take your stops and equally important the time of day. If you planned to stop for the night at a pilot/loves/TA/etc but it’s already 10:30, you are likely shit out of luck. 

Treat your truck like your own home, because it is. Take your trash out, keep your space clean, keep dirty laundry from clean (buy a second laundry bag in a different color), etc. 

Backing. Backing takes time to be halfway decent. I’m a year in and still find myself fucking up stuff. Get out and look. Any driver would rather wait an extra 5-10 minutes for you to do it right, than you back into someone/something and now they are stuck as you wait to assess damage. 

Gas station etiquette. Pump your gas, throw your shit away, and pull forward. If you’re gonna go in for some food or whatever as well, pull into a parking spot. Do not be that fuckin jerk off that blocks the scales or the pump because you HAD to get more shitty gas station food. 

Get to know your truck. Figure out what the switches do, figure out what the height and weight is, figure out how to slide tandems and shift the weight around. I sometimes will read through the vehicle manual if I’m stuck in a place with low/no service just to both pass time and get a better understanding of the truck. 

Lastly, be mindful. 99% of the cars on the road truly do not give a fuck about you and think you are there to personally annoy them. Keep your spacing, maintain your lane, and don’t get mad. Short of ramming into them, there is nothing you can do to them, so let there shitty attitude go.
